The authors propose novel representations for logical containment and the converse relationship between principles. These novel representations are reflect fundamental properties of logical relationships and can be translated into established notions via established proof-theoretic connections. The article introduces novel notions such as "for all" and "there exists" semantic operators and explores their link to Herbrand disjunctions and the semi-interpretability of first-order logic. The authors also identify key features that any adequate foundational concept for logic should possess.

Reward learning systems struggle due to limited data, so expanding the dataset
doesn't necessarily improve their performance. Instead, organizing the data
into meaningful groups can aid the learning process. Batching related experiences
and gathering distinct comparisons can accelerate the learning rate by reducing
unnecessary comparisons. Nonetheless, successfully creating these comparison
groups is complicated and often results in comparisons that are irrelevant or
obvious. To resolve this, we've developed a system to curate more productive
comparisons through analysis of human feedback. By collecting feedback on the
performance of different policies in varied scenarios, we're able to group tasks
in a way that human feedback finds more policy comparisons relevant. We've seen
through experiments that this approach results in more productive human feedback
by increasing the ratio of task-groupings to comparisons collected to total
possible comparisons of 14:1, as well as improving overall performance with a 12%
enhancement as measured by the final achieved reward. By maximizing the impact
of human feedback, we're able to focus limited resources on the most crucial
aspects of the reward learning process.

The Smyth powerspace formulation was initially designed to capture the essence of core-compact structures, but it doesn't consistently preserve this property. We explore modifications to the Smyth powerspace that maintain core-compact properties by incorporating upper bounds into its definition. These modified powerspaces are equivalent to certain types of Cech-Stone compactifications. We demonstrate that for certain classes of structures, the original Smyth powerspace does preserve core-compact properties, resolving previously open questions.

The theory of vortex loops allows us to examine the behavior of ideal 2D fluids. In this context, we define a pointed vortex loop as a loop with a designated starting point that encompasses a finite area. The space of all possible vortex loops with a given strength includes distinct regions, including ones with the topological characteristics of a sphere, a torus, or various other types. We demonstrate that when the loop's strength is low enough, the space surrounding these configurations is homeomorphic to the space of all possible ways a knot can be configured. The evidence supporting this claim involves showing that as two low-strength vortex loops approach each other, they behave in a similar way to two knots approaching each other. Furthermore, our findings also suggest that the loop space for a finite number of co-prime strengths is homeomorphic to a torus. We also discuss how this result can be extended to higher-dimensional analogs of vortex loops, known as higher-dimensional loop spaces and utilize a modified version of the Brownian motion technique to achieve this extension.

We have investigated the Asymptotic Invariant Profit-Wise AIPW estimator, introducing a novel approach by Taylor-Expanding around a non-regularized version of the AIPW objective under continuous risk minimization. Our analysis highlights the impact of regularization and the limitations of the estimator when risks are not strictly convex. Empirical results are presented on imbalanced click data from Google, showing improvements in inversions and click predictions when incorporating the AIPW estimator.

The European Physical Journal C published a letter outlining plans for a new lattice study, focusing on the tau particle's decay into a kaon, a lepton, and a neutrino. This research aims to determine the reliability of theoretical predictions essential for understanding the Standard Model's consistency and future probes of beyond-Standard-Model physics. Due to the tau's relatively light mass, it is well-suited for lattice Monte Carlo simulations, making this a vital project for enhancing theoretical precision in this area.

Researchers investigated how baroclinic waves in a rotating, vertical annulus behave by examining surface phenomena using direct observation and related techniques like hot-wire measurements and flow visualization. The study focused on a strong baroclinic vortex with significant horizontal and vertical temperature differences, characterized by intense, large-scale circulations and small-scale, high-frequency flows. The surface temperature gradient displayed complex, non-repeating patterns, closely related to high-speed, high-frequency flows. The temperature difference distribution changed over time, with the largest variations occurring at high speeds, and their movement followed a non-repeating path. The researchers used flow visualization to study the thermal structure and its interaction with the circulation. They found that the thermal aspect would reverse just before reaching the outer wall of the annulus, while the circulation would change direction just after the inner wall. The time it took for the thermal aspect to complete a cycle (outer to inner) was almost the same as the time it took for the circulation to complete a cycle (inner to outer). The speed of the thermal aspect was approximately half the speed of the circulation.

We investigate Bayesian estimation for extreme value models using the Lognormal-Gaussian Hybrid (LNGH) model and introduce a novel approach to select the underlying tuning parameter, currently chosen arbitrarily. Utilizing a hierarchical Bayesian framework, our method allows the tuning parameter to vary during the estimation process. Due to the model's complexity, encompassing a non-differentiable likelihood and a heavy-tailed prior, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation is employed to sample from the posterior distribution. Within a detailed numerical study, the impact of the tuning parameter is explored, and its behavior is analyzed. Furthermore, the performance of our model is assessed on various real-world datasets, comparing it to alternative extreme value models.

We investigate reinforcement learning in a corrupted environment where an aggressive adversary intentionally generates opaque reward signals to mislead the learner. Owing to the challenge posed by the corruption, even the most efficient reinforcement learning algorithms can struggle to adapt. Notably, we find that knowing the level of corruption, denoted as $\epsilon$, enables us to create robust algorithms. For certain corrupting strategies, we design an algorithm that recovers rewards while incurring only a minor time and statistical cost, even when the corruption extent is significant. This algorithm is applicable in a variety of corruption models and can be adapted for other scenarios where the corruption extent is unknown. Furthermore, we show that not being aware of the corruption level leads to a significant increase in the time and statistical cost, leading to a separation between orders in terms of efficiency. We propose a sample-efficient approach to estimate the corruption level and demonstrate its applicability. We also explore the possibility of detecting corruption by analyzing the policy's performance on corrupted rewards. Notably, we observe that robust learning often necessitates exploiting regularities in transition dynamics, which we discovered through a correlation analysis between the rewards and the actions taken by the corrupting agent. This leads to the design of a new attack strategy, dubbed the'reward-shifting attack,' which targets the most frequent states and regularities in the environment. We provide empirical evidence to demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms against the worst possible attacks in several robotic domains.

This research examines the controllability of the impulsive heat equation, a semi-discrete model that incorporates discrete, sporadic control interventions. The study's primary goal is to investigate the impact of these impulses on the equation's controllability. The authors demonstrate that small increments in initial conditions can lead to controllability, under specific time and space parameter constraints. A new approach to solving the impulsive heat equation involves a two-step method: the iterative decomposition of a successive difference equation, followed by the application of a fixed-point theorem. The resulting fixed point can be used to develop a successive difference equation with controllable inputs, facilitating the extension of the study's findings to the impulsive heat equation. The findings suggest that impulse control can improve the equation's regularity, making it more amenable to control. The authors also establish the relationship between impulse control and the discrete, sporadic oscillations that can arise in finite difference approximations of parabolic equations.

Detectors for out-of-distribution (OoD) detections face significant challenges when confronted with unlabeled data from unfamiliar sources. Existing methods often rely on comparative analyses between known and unknown data distributions. However, these comparative approaches fall short in cases where the source domains differ substantially. Notably, many of these methods struggle with unknown data from the ImageNet dataset. Given the importance of accurate OoD detection in evaluating the reliability of vision models, the need for improvements is pressing. In response, we develop a novel method called Unknown-Pretermit (UP). UP incorporates an unknown classifier that disregards predictions on unfamiliar data rather than making potentially inaccurate predictions. Upcoming Section 3 provides further details on UP. Notably, UP is distinct from other neural network regularization techniques in that it aims to mitigate errors rather than constrain behavior. In experiments, we evaluate the effectiveness of UP on various benchmark datasets and uncover that it surpasses comparative methods on known OoD data while achieving comparable performance on unknown data. The evaluation is summarized in Table 1 and Figure 1. In contrast, comparative approaches underperform on unknown data from challenge sets, including those from ImageNet and CIFAR-10. In contrast, UP exhibits superior performance on these challenge sets. In addition to these experiments, we perform ablation studies on the performance of UP and provide details on hyperparameter settings in Section 4. We suggest investigating the dynamics of molecular motors driven by rotary motion, by incorporating an external force induced by a carbon nanotube probe. This force, caused by the nanotube's velocity, can be studied using existing simulations of scanning force microscopy. By analyzing the resulting motor-probe interaction, it's possible to gain insights into how the motor utilizes energy from ATP hydrolysis to counteract this force, thus propelling itself forward. This research could provide a link between theoretical models of molecular motors and actual experimental measurements.

A one-way tape rewriting machine and a two-way tape rewriting machine with restricted jump ability are examined in this study, where only forward jumps are possible from the starting point. It's demonstrated in this study that any two-way word transducer with a limited number of non-deterministic states can be replaced by a synchronized one-way transducer with a specified reset symbol, using a bounded and regular reset sequence. Conversely, it's shown that there are instances of non-deterministic two-way tape rewriting machines that cannot be equivalent to any forward-jumping two-way tape rewriting machine, and also cannot be equivalent to any one-way tape rewriting machine with a reset symbol. A significant result of this study is that any non-deterministic two-way word transducer with a limited number of states can be replaced by a forward-jumping two-way word transducer with a limited number of states, and also that any non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be replaced by a bounded and regular one-way transducer with a reset symbol.

Our research focuses on the $f$-Convolution, a fundamental operation in wavelet theory that has an approximate time complexity of $O(n \log^3 n)$. This paper presents an algorithm to efficiently calculate a single entry of the $f$-Convolution with an approximate time complexity of $O(n \log^2 n)$. This improvement allows for faster convolution-based wavelet transform construction, reducing the time complexity from $O(n \log^3 n)$ to $O(n \log^2 n)$.

We have carried out atmospheric analysis of GJ 229B, a sub-brown dwarf on a wide-separation close-in binary system, following up on its initial discovery in 1995. GJ 229B's atmosphere was examined using cross-correlation analysis of its transmission spectrum, obtained through the use of the WFC3 on board the Hubble Space Telescope. This study has provided us with the knowledge that GJ 229B's effective temperature does not exceed 1400 K and that it has a composition similar to solar abundance. This research has also set a limit on the atmospheric metallicity of GJ 229B, ranging from log[Metals]/H=-1.98 to -1.54. The atmosphere of GJ 229B examined in this study is likely to be dynamic and varies over time. The variability of its atmospheric metallicity may be caused by formation condensates over time. This is the first known sub-brown dwarf or exoplanet with such a composition profile. The study of intermediate objects between planets and stars is crucial in understanding the processes of formation and evolution. The atmospheric analysis of GJ 229B, a sub-brown dwarf with a wide-separation close-in binary system, has provided us with information on its temperature and composition. A detailed study into the nature of heavy-light mesons and their constituent parts is conducted using lattice QCD with an emphasis on understanding the tetraquark spectrum. This research investigates how various quark masses and gauge field configurations contribute to the meson mass spectrum and the correlation functions that represent it. The findings reveal significant differences between the four-quark correlation functions associated with tetraquark states and those linked to meson bound states. This distinction is utilized to develop a spectral density, a theoretical concept derived from the Korolla formula, which predicts the presence of tetraquark states at certain calculable points. The analysis also considers how various factors, such as quark mass and lattice size, affect this density and the resulting tetraquark spectrum. The importance of these factors and their impact on the accuracy of the spectral density and resulting tetraquark spectrum are discussed in detail.

We examine the possibility that $C
eq P$ violation in kaon decays is significantly influenced by new physics. Using the Standard Model prediction for the $C
eq P$-violating phase $\phi_{e}^{(s)}$, we can better understand the potential constraints of experimental results. Our research specifically explores how a unitary triangle with a narrow angle $	heta_{K}^{m SM}$ might be formed. Even a slight deviation from the Standard Model prediction for $\phi_{e}^{(s)}$ could result in a substantial change in the constraint for new physics parameters. A precise measurement of the $C
eq P$-violating phase within the Standard Model will significantly enhance our ability to detect new physics in $C
eq P$-violating processes.

Initially, simple models like the well-mixed model were used to predict aerosol spread. However, there's growing evidence that these models don't accurately reflect real-world aerosol dynamics. More complex simulations, such as those involving turbulence, are now being employed to inform infection prevention measures. We examine the validity of using the well-mixed model to estimate aerosol concentrations likely to be inhaled by others, given that the model assumes uniform mixing and ignores various turbulence influences. We compare the model's predictions to those of detailed airflow simulations in a range of environments including closed spaces, open areas, and spaces with mixed airflow conditions. The objective is to determine the model's limitations, providing insights that can inform policy decisions during public health emergencies while also highlighting the need for more accurate predictive tools.

The 7-neutron isotopes of Te isotone nuclei exhibit unique properties tied to their nuclear prolate deformation, which is characterized by the presence of single-particle states. Researchers utilized a large-data set of (β, γ)-transitions derived from high-energy γ-ray spectra, which were measured across a range of isotones, including 135Te and 137Te. These studies revealed insight into the structure of these nuclei. The analysis started by standardizing the transition intensity calculation method, which involves considering the feed-in contribution, across the entire series of Te isotones. The analysis of transition patterns in this group allowed researchers to identify patterns in the deformation properties of 135Te and 137Te. The studies also demonstrated that the 2011 year survey data aligns with more recent studies, including those conducted with proton and anti-proton induced beams.

This research presents a set of advanced theorems that enable the precise detection of violations within exchange programs. Exchange programs are a crucial component in processing database queries, and their efficient checking has been a major challenge. While previous works can only identify a few specific types of violations, our new findings allow for the automatic detection of a wide range of violations, and this improved capability is achieved through a novel mathematical approach that guarantees accuracy and efficiency. Moreover, our approach enables the detection of violations in programs that were previously thought to be immune to such violations, and it also provides a general method for verifying the correctness of programs. This improved capability is achieved through a novel mathematical approach that enables the detection of programs that were previously thought to be immune to such violations, and it also provides a general method for verifying the correctness of programs.

The masses of the bottom mesons in $F$-wave have been predicted using the light-front wave functions and light-front QCD sum rules. It was found that the mesons sharing the same quantum numbers as the $B^0$ particle are called $F$-wave bottom mesons. By solving the light-front QCD equations, the light-front wave functions of these mesons were obtained. Using the energy-momentum tensor, light-front QCD sum rules were applied to calculate their masses. The results showed that the predictions of the two methods agree well with each other and exhibit a Regges trajectory, indicating that the excitation energies of the mesons depend on the angular momenta.

We examine whether Szabados's conjecture about minimal periodic decompositions holds for specific patterns, which he initially suspected to be true. To this end, we have discovered that the conjecture is indeed true for all patterns consisting of a single element, but it is also false for more complex patterns that consist of two elements. By analyzing the differences between these patterns, we have developed a new method for obtaining sharp upper limits on the number of periods in these decompositions.

A mathematical decomposition technique called Dynamic Mode Decomposition is widely used in numerous fields to extract significant behavior from complex system data, especially when the system itself is complex. However, traditional DMD struggles to accurately represent the nonlinear aspects of many real-world systems. To overcome this limitation, a new kernel-based DMD method was developed, which effectively captures the nonlinear relationships in data by transforming it into a linear space before applying the DMD algorithm. The proposed kernel DMD method was compared to the standard DMD and spatio-temporal DMD on several challenging test cases, and it significantly outperformed them by correctly identifying the nonlinear system dynamics and providing a stable and interpretable outcome.

The evaluation of chess openings and player talent has long been a subject of interest, but also a significant challenge, as it involves intricate aspects of the game. To address this issue, an innovative approach is proposed in this article, where the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm is applied to analyze the strategies. This dynamic system continuously adjusts its rules in accordance with the performance of the best and worst players, effectively mirroring the evolution of chess variations. As a result, the analysis reveals distinct regions within the fitness landscape, where the skills of top players are highly effective. Notably, data from top chess tournaments confirms that players with higher ratings occupy the upper layers of this complex structure. To achieve this outcome, a sophisticated statistical technique, known as the Multivariate Fokker-Planck equation, is utilized to simulate the movement of player skills across the fitness landscape. This theoretical model is then validated using real-game data, where the distribution of player positions is observed to converge over time to match the distribution observed in the fitness landscape.

In the context of binary systems consisting of a neutron star and a white dwarf, Accretion Induced Collapse occurs when the addition of mass to either star leads to a catastrophic collapse into a more compact object, typically a black hole or a more stable neutron star. Depending on the final state, such events are considered candidates to explain the observed properties of heavy neutron stars. For processes involving a final stable neutron star, it's estimated that the majority of material from both stars is ejected during the Disintegration of the Neutron Star due to thermal pressures. However, the ultimate fate of the initially compact object, determined by core properties, remains unchanged. Conversely, a final black hole outcome results in the total loss of material from both stars as detected in a Microquasar Emission. Prior studies focused on the impact of magnetic interactions between the two objects, assuming a shared plane and aligned rotations. Yet, it's now recognized that such assumptions may not always be valid. This research aims to investigate variations in Accretion Induced Collapse scenarios by considering diverse initial conditions, while also accounting for the effects of magnetic forces and differing assumptions about the objects' rotational axes and their respective orbits.

The Euler-Lagrange equation is a fourth or higher-order nonlinear ODE, often found in physical systems like the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator. We have developed a method to find a first integrals for these Euler-Lagrange equations and represented them in a symbolic form. A specific condition allows the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator to be transformed into a quarter-order Hamiltonian ODE, revealing a first integrals and new symmetry principles in the process.

Three-dimensional shape retrieval is a complex problem in geometry and computer vision. Various methods have been proposed to match sketch-based queries with 3D objects. However, existing approaches primarily focus on local geometric features, which may not fully capture the sketch's global, abstract characteristics. To address this limitation, we develop a novel architecture for 3D sketch retrieval, featuring a global encoder that effectively captures both global and local shape features from input sketches. A comparative study on multiple datasets reveals our method surpasses prior art in performance. Moreover, we present a device for generating abstract 3D sketches, which serves as a benchmark, rather than generating precise 3D models as in traditional approaches.

The planet HD80606b, a highly eccentric world with extremely close approaches to its star, offers an unique opportunity to observe its atmosphere responding to heat. In 2011, astronomers employed Spitzer and Hubble telescopes to monitor the planet's temperature as it orbits its star, and to their surprise, they observed the expected heating effect, but also an unexpected rapid temperature drop as it approaches the star. Recent models suggest that the gas in the surrounding environment can absorb the planet's thermal radiation, causing the temperature to appear higher than it should be. Researchers have now taken this phenomenon into account, and have shown that the net effect is a smaller than previously thought temperature difference, and that the planet's distance from its star is better matched by models taking this process into account.

Researchers observed a viscosity-free fluid's collapse into a black hole for the first time in the Center of the Galaxy. They simulated a point mass at the galaxy's center, representing a supermassive black hole, and used realistic equations to model the surrounding gas and stars. Despite the massive black hole, the galaxy's center's density is very low, but it does not need to be zero for the phenomenon of a collapsing fluid forming a singularity to occur. Even small deviations from an idealized mass distribution can prevent the singularity from appearing. Additionally, it may be possible for a rotating fluid to collapse into a black hole without angular momentum, and it has been shown that this process can occur with different types of spins.

The weak gravity conjecture suggests that in a higher-dimensional black hole ensemble, the entropy of an extremal black hole should be proportional to its mass. This theory can be tested using a canonical ensemble by first freezing the angular momentum of the black hole, then changing its size to see the resulting changes in mass and entropy. A new method has been developed to do this efficiently for more complex black holes and used to investigate the properties of a five-dimensional black ring. Our findings indicate that the weak gravity conjecture is satisfied when the freezing angle is greater than or equal to the charge-dependent angle associated with the Asymptotic AdS 3-Century Entropy, but not when it is lower. Furthermore, the results show that the third law of black hole mechanics holds as predicted by the hypothesis of the weak gravity conjecture.

Autonomous reinforcement learning systems can now be achieved by combining a novel intrinsic motivation module with external performance incentives, which can significantly reduce training time. We've developed a intrinsic motivation module, derived from Autoregressive Modular Complex Autonomous Systems, which learns to generate effective goal states for intrinsic purpose. We've also discovered that providing a limited amount of external motivation along with intrinsic rewards is more effective than either alone, resulting in faster training times than when only intrinsic rewards are used. We've tested this approach on a variety of tasks, including image generation and basic game playing, which demonstrates its efficiency.

Coloured Poincaré gravity, an extension of the Poincaré algebra for gauge fields, is explored in this research. It distinguishes itself as a distinct subset within the coloured version of the conformal algebra, characterised by the absence of a conformal transformation. A D-dimensional coloured Poincaré gravity model is developed, incorporating both massive and massless particle types, whose gauge fields are represented by multi-coloured, symmetric and anti-symmetric tensors. These are described by respective colour-structured generalised Poincaré algebras and invariance groups. A brief discussion on possible spin-1/2 matter models is also provided.

We propose a parameterized family of algorithms for directed acyclic graphs based on their free-set parameter, analyzing how the family scales with treewidth, vertex cover, and pathwidth. Essentially, this parameter represents how "thin" a graph is in a particular direction. Our findings show that:

- We can solve the Clique-Deletion problem in directed acyclic graphs in $O(c^k + c \cdot k)$ time, with an optimal $c=2^{O(t)}$. This problem asks how many cliques of a specific size can be removed from a graph to prevent any remaining subgraph from having a cliques of that size in it.
- We can solve the Vertex-Deletion problem in directed acyclic graphs in $O(c^k + c \cdot k)$ time, with an optimal $c=2^{O(tw)}$. This problem asks how many vertices can be removed from a graph to make a specified number of vertices in a particular size gone.
- We can solve the H-Vertex-Deletion problem in directed acyclic graphs in $O(c^k + c \cdot kw)$ time, with an optimal $c=2^{O(tw)}$. This problem asks how many vertices can be removed from a graph to make a specified number of vertices in a particular size gone, with constraints on how those vertices can be selected.
- We can solve the Clique-Deletion problem on graphs of pathwidth at most $k

The A\* algorithm is the foundation for many navigation systems, ensuring the fastest path to a destination by following established rules. However, these basic rules are often blind to obstacles and can result in unnecessary detours. Previous research attempted to address this issue, but largely focused on specific environments, such as labyrinths or dynamic situations, leading to limited universal applications. In contrast, we propose MemoNav, a more efficient model that builds upon A\* with a dynamic memory mechanism and transfer learning capabilities. By maintaining a record of significant obstacles and their connections, our model enables the discovery of new paths that avoid repeated detours. Additionally, by leveraging ongoing and past experiences, our model accelerates the learning process and achieves improved results compared to traditional A\* and deep learning-based models. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in challenging scenarios, such as navigating through Cornelia Island and a city street layout in Santa Monica, while also exhibiting enhanced invariance to various transformations, such as rotations and scaling.

In the context of 5G New Radio and future cellular technologies, the millimeter wave (mmW) spectrum and the unlicensed 60 GHz band are gaining significant attention. To optimize wireless systems in crowded urban environments, this paper proposes a joint channel sensing and power allocation technique based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL). The author's approach combines an actor-critic DRL architecture to both identify available spectrum channels and distribute power across multiple user equipment (UEs), with a focus on maximizing their respective data transfer rates. The proposed method is evaluated using a comprehensive urban mmW simulator and compared with state-of-the-art techniques.

The majority of models examining active dynamics and collective behavior focus on local interactions, but this work investigates the effects of long-range interactions and diffusive coupling on active dynamics, using a simple model that yields spatially heterogeneous solutions. Analysis shows that these interactions give rise to a widespread, active state characterised by numerous patterns, including stripes, dots, and random distributions. Locations of active sites are mapped in dimensionless parameters space, and according to different scenarios, patterns either disappear as system dynamics change, or switch between different configurations. The stability of these patterns is evaluated through linear stability analysis and numerical simulations, and according to different scenarios, some patterns exhibit a phase transition into stability, while others remain stable across all possible parameter combinations. The work concludes with an assessment of how these results compare to other, related models.

The rate at which symmetry properties are lost and operators mix is a crucial characteristic of how information grows in quantum systems over time. By utilizing the symmetries present in the system, we can significantly reduce the complexity of calculating these mixing rates. We achieve this by exploiting the symmetry properties in the Hilbert space basis, which allows us to compute the mixing rates through a simpler symmetry- constrained matrix growth problem. We demonstrate this by applying the symmetry to the mixing matrix, which becomes block-diagonal, consisting of matrices representing different symmetry groups. The primary focus is on $U(1)$ symmetry, and we derive the symmetry-constrained matrix growth equation for this case. The resulting mixed state correlation functions provide a clearer view of the operator mixing process. Moreover, the symmetry in the correlation functions' growth rate is preserved, and we find that the maximum mixing occurs within the same symmetry group. Applying this to the Triviality order of the O(2) symmetry group, we find that the mixing rates transition from minimal to maximal at a critical time. Similarly, we analyze the $SU(N)_1$ symmetry and find that the mixing rates peak and then decline as it progresses.

Theoretical analysis focusing on the 7.65 MeV Hoyle state's decay within $^{12}$C is conducted with a non-sequential decay model that incorporates the systematic characteristics of $^{11}$C's ground state and 2.84 MeV 5/2$^{-}$ state. Calculations that consider only one non-sequential decay amplitude are able to reproduce the observed 1/sqrt(2) angular correlation pattern following the emission of a proton from the Hoyle state, providing a good fit to experimental data across a range of energy resolutions. This analysis highlights the significance of including the 2.84 MeV 11$^{o}$+ state in $^{11}$C's wave function to describe the Hoyle state. Our study's results are presented with energy resolutions replicating those found in recent experiments, offering insights into the decay process's structure. Our model also predicts a non-sequential decay component representing 11% of the total Hoyle state's decay to the ground state of $^{11}$C, with implications that need to be considered in the analysis of future experimental data using the Double Chooz or STOLI experiments.

Brittle material fracture patterns remain largely observational and the underlying fracture mechanics are not entirely understood. The presence of intrinsic length scales in these materials complicate fracture dynamics, leading to computationally challenging predictions. A new study reveals that when these length scales exceed a critical value, crack propagation becomes stable under high loading speeds, occurring in a stable periodic pattern. The research utilizes a computational model that combines continuum mechanics with a damage model and the Coarse-Grained Molecular Statistics method to simulate damage growth. The findings show that stable cracks only occur at certain sizes of these length scales. The predicted stable cracks match observations in nature and experiments, offering a framework for designing fracture-resistant materials at a microscopic level.

This study delves into channel capacity caused by implicit knowledge of past constraints. The investigation centers on a single user communication system, where the encoder has access to causal state information, and the decoder knows this information with a delay. Based on this framework, the network's capacity is examined and compared with its non-causal counterpart. The analysis involves computing the capacity of an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel with a state constraint, and it's discovered that introducing temporal disparities results in diminished capacity. Moreover, the total amount of past information the channel can hold is found to be directly proportional to the square root of the delay. The findings are further extended by considering multiple users, where the interaction between delay and multi-user effects is explored.

In materials that exhibit both superconductivity and significant spin-orbit coupling, the combination of interactions often results in a trivial superconducting state transitioning directly from a topological band structure. The C54Ir4Pt4 unit in the high-temperature superconductor family, specifically in compound C56Fe4Pt4-0.5K2Cr3Si5 (with 0.5K2Cr3Si5 being an antiferromagnetic host), provides a suitable platform to study the interaction between spin-orbit effects and superconductivity. Utilizing a four-terminal transport measurement technique, the C56Ir4Pt4 compound was discovered to maintain topological properties even at low temperatures, found to be a Weyl-point superconductor with secured quantization of Majorana zero modes via precise numerical analysis. The unique properties of this compound make it an ideal subject for further study in the field of topological superconductivity research.

In 2021, SEM-TAB-FACTS introduced a challenge with four sub-tasks that prompted researchers to extract specific entities and facts from medical seminar papers. Held in conjunction with the NAACL 2021 conference, the competition drew 18 participants who submitted a combined total of 4500 validated responses across its four sub-tasks, achieving particularly high success rates in sub-tasks focused on extracting author and institutional information. Recent progress in pre-trained language models has been shown to enhance performance on this task, and our analysis provides further insights into what contributes to successful results.

This paper presents a fundamental critique of Quantum Mechanics by incorporating historical perspective and explanatory modeling. A key point of contention revolves around the exclusion of complex numbers, a point that was particularly contentious between Einstein and Bohr. In pursuit of resolution, this paper introduces a novel approach based on an old theory known as Pilot-Wave Hydrodynamics, developed by Louis de Broglie and David Bohm. Pilot-Wave Hydrodynamics offers a simple and well-explained model that can address common criticisms leveled against Quantum Mechanics, including its inability to reconcile position and momentum principles. However, this model is hindered by the non-reflexive nature of its corresponding mathematical framework. Nonetheless, the model presents a compelling case that suggests Quantum Mechanics may be viewed as an inaccurate approximation of Pilot-Wave Hydrodynamics when particles become sufficiently small. Such an understanding could facilitate a fresh reconciliation of theoretical physics, encompassing General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics, by drawing on Pilot-Wave Hydrodynamics' inherent non-local properties.

Given a connected, undirected graph G and a real number t ≥ 0, the t-geodesic distance on G is the smallest integer k such that any two vertices of G have a path connecting them in G whose length in G is less or equal to t, or INFINITY if there's no such path in G that doesn't exceed t. The Wolkowitz distance on G is the maximum of the geodesic distance on G for all vertices in G. The geodesic distance and the Wolkowitz distance on G are both important concepts in the study of G. In this paper, the author studies the metric dimension of a graph G and the Wolkowitz distance on G. The author first proves that there's a real number tp such that the metric dimension of G doesn't change when the geodesic distance on G is less or equal to tp, but changes otherwise. This tp is the smallest number tp such that any vertex in G has a path connecting it to any other vertex in G with length in G at most tp. This tp is also the largest number tp such that any vertex in G has a path connecting it to any other vertex in G with length in G that doesn't exceed tp. The steady-state flow equation can be simplified by integrating pressures vertically, assuming a constant gradient in hydraulic conductivity across the ground. This approach provides accurate results when hydraulic conductivity is uniform throughout the entire medium. However, it becomes less accurate in layers with significantly varying hydraulic conductivities. By using numerical integration, the vertical flow equation can be accurately solved even in complex geologic formations where hydraulic conductivity changes drastically at every layer. In this study, we derive an analytical solution for steady-state flow in a two-dimensional system with varying hydraulic conductivity on a specific type of layer called a layered triangular formation. This result can be used to modify numerical models for modeling groundwater flow and to validate numerical methods for such applications.

This research project's primary goal was to investigate the feasibility of the O3-UV technology for removing air pollutants such as VOCs and SO2 from flue gases produced by cement kilns. The O3-UV process was tested in a cylindrical reactor with a volume of 50 liters, using oxygen-rich flue gases and various VOCs as the target substances. The results showed that sulfur dioxide could be completely removed within certain reactor configurations, with a high positive correlation between reactor size and reaction rate, and a moderate correlation with concentration. The oxidation of hydrocarbons was found to be highly dependent on concentration, with lower reaction rates observed at lower concentrations, and a positive correlation with temperature, ranging from 22°C to 42°C.

As the demand for compute-intensive artificial intelligence continues to grow, novel types of highly efficient virtual computing platforms are in high demand. To meet this need, we have designed a new approach to virtual platform segmentation, where a complex compute environment is broken down into simpler, connected modules to optimize performance. We have developed a framework for generating virtual platforms with multiple layers of segmentation, where each layer is optimized for different performance metrics. We tested this approach by creating three different architectures for a neuromorphic accelerator and simulating their performance using system-level languages. Our results show that by segmenting the platform into software components, we can reduce simulation times from hours to minutes, with some configurations achieving a 7.8x speedup. We found that platform segmentation has a significant impact on simulation efficiency and that different architectures can result in substantial time savings with no trade-off in accuracy.

We introduce Indecision Trees, an innovative variant of Decision Trees that incorporates deliberate uncertainty into the learning process. By purposefully limiting model accuracy, Indecision Trees create opportunities for optimization techniques to improve performance. This research investigates the effectiveness of utilizing Indecision Trees as a feature reduction and data augmentation method. Our analysis examines the benefits of Indecision Trees on multiple benchmark datasets, revealing improvements in classification performance and enhanced feature selection capabilities. Furthermore, Indecision Trees demonstrate competitiveness when compared to established methods in various machine learning tasks. Notably, Indecision Trees exhibit a notable advantage in computational efficiency, with inference and training processes accelerated by a factor of at least 3 and 2, respectively, when compared to alternative approaches.

The problem of time series similarity search has significant implications across multiple domains, including healthcare and environmental monitoring. Due to the massive scale of related data, search operations are often painstakingly slow. This research aims to enhance the search efficiency by allowing queries to abandon the comparison process early, much like the popular ANNOY library does. To achieve this, we introduce a novel variant of the ball tree data structure, incorporating approximate radius-based queries. This approach involves the utilization of MH-distances during query execution to facilitate early abandonment. Additionally, we optimize ball tree construction by utilizing a modified clone tree data structure and reducing memory consumption via path downsizing. These improvements result in significant search speedup and reduced memory requirements when compared to existing libraries, including ball tree, ball M-tree, and ANNOY. This research further addresses key performance indicators such as search efficiency, training time, and data structure size.

Recent research on automated grading has focused on creating ideal types of feedback to give to students when evaluating their code submissions. Nevertheless, there's still no clear understanding of whether providing various kinds of feedback affects students' learning or coding abilities. This study aims to address this question by exploring how different types of feedback influence students' performance, using a combination of multiple code analyzers to simulate various feedback types and assign scores for their submissions. We found that providing detailed, explicit feedback tends to improve code coverage and ultimately scores, although it doesn't necessarily increase submission quality. This suggests that providing such feedback may have a positive impact on programming skills. Additionally, we discovered that using multiple code analyzers can help improve grading accuracy and reduce errors compared to relying on a single analyzer.

In recent years, decision-making algorithms relying on intricate, impossible-to-interpret models have become prevalent. To facilitate better comprehension of these algorithms, researchers have developed various approaches to shed light on the decision-making processes of such models. This study proposes a novel approach, known as Surrogate-Aided Probing (SAP), which utilizes simplified, symbolic models to understand and explain the decisions made by complex, black-box classifiers. SAP achieves this by generating and leveraging simplified models, such as logical formulas or decision trees, to represent the original classifier. This representation enables a detailed analysis of the decision-making algorithm, including the identification of crucial input variables and the optimization of variables to influence the algorithm's output. The study demonstrates SAP's effectiveness by applying it to two real-world, real-estate market datasets.

Over-smoothing is a well-documented issue in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), where information is progressively lost as the message-passing process continues. This problem has been addressed by several methods that aim to prevent over-smoothing by restricting information exchange or developing new architectures. However, the underlying causes of over-smoothing remain unclear, hindering the design of effective solutions. In this study, we investigate the factors contributing to over-smoothing and develop a framework to mitigate this issue. By exploring the effects of network architectures and training procedures, we identify key parameters that influence over-smoothing and make unexpected observations about the causes of progressive information loss. To this end, we propose a new technique - ProGAT, a procedural graph attention network architecture, designed to prevent over-smoothing and maintain key information across multiple propagation steps. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the efficacy of ProGAT in outperforming existing methods and providing accurate generalization on GraphNet and GraphConv architectures even after several propagation steps. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw2/ProGAT.git.

We analyze simplified models of dark matter production via mediator decay or mediation in a complex loop process, focusing on dark matter and a gauge boson emergence. To streamline the analysis, we select the most relevant mediator types and representation for the dark matter particle. We produce constraints on the simplified models using the LHC dark matter search data from experiments such as CMS and ATLAS, as well as with the LUX-ZEPLIN dark matter direct detection data. We show that future dark matter direct detection experiments like next-generation LXe-based detectors may impose the most restrictive limits on the simplified models. We also find that future LHC dark matter searches, particularly with higher luminosity data, will significantly impact our understanding of the simplified models.

We introduce a set of eight new functions of one variable, aimed at describing the transverse motion of quarks and gluons within hadrons. These functions will be extractable from data related to jet production processes, specifically from interactions involving high-energy particles, and are anticipated to provide valuable insights into the internal transverse structures of quarks and gluons. Furthermore, functions of this type will be sensitive to the effects of internal color dipole screening that occurs at high energies, a phenomenon not currently accounted for in theoretical models. Our analysis involves identifying the functions, determining their physical properties, and outlining the procedures for extracting them from data through a comparative study of data and theoretical models. Our investigations indicate that functions of this type can be highly sensitive to factors such as internal transverse momentum distributions and color dipole attachment probabilities. Moreover, we find that while certain functions may be highly correlated with one another, their unique roles within the set provides opportunities for extracting valuable information about the internal transverse structures of quarks and gluons.

This research demonstrates that specific products, including those involving the Closed Long Ray and Long Line with a wide array of compact abelian groups, along with Tree Shaped Spaces, exhibit the Compactly Supported Homeomorphism Property. Furthermore, it is shown that for these products, a compactly supported homeomorphism can be designed to preserve compact support.

The unique properties of graphene make it an ideal substrate for growing a variety of epitaxial materials. Monolayers of epitaxial semiconductor materials, such as germanium and tin, can be grown on graphene while maintaining a direct contact, which is beneficial for creating new electronic devices. However, research has revealed that the chemical interaction between graphene and these semiconductor materials results in distinct growth patterns across different regions, which are influenced by factors such as temperature, chemical composition, and coverage. In this study, we examined the geometric structures of germanium nanowires through high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and identified different epitaxial domains that are formed during growth. In ultra-high vacuum conditions, germanium nanowires formed a square pattern, while those grown with molecular beam epitaxy at higher temperatures displayed a triangular structure. Notably, this triangular shape resembled a well-known structure found in single-layer graphene called a moire pattern, which suggests a strong interaction between graphene and germanium. In contrast, the square pattern was observed to be the result of a weaker chemical interaction between graphene and germanium. In atmospheric pressure, the germanium nanowires exhibited a unique rod-packing structure that is similar to a graphene moire pattern. These findings provide the first evidence of the growth of semiconductor materials that are strongly interacting with graphene and may lead to new ways to grow new electronic materials.

This study offers an innovative approach to detecting the shared trends present in multiple time-series data sets, particularly suited for analyzing large data sets with complex patterns. The method provides reliable estimates of the number of common trends, is resistant to outliers, and can be easily extended to accommodate additional variables. The proposed estimator is robust and efficient, yielding precise results even at the sample size equivalent to twice the number of observations in a typical model. The method's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art techniques under standard conditions and outperforms them significantly in scenarios involving extreme data points. The findings are further supported by simulations and real-world data examples.

Galaxy cluster lensing analysis has primarily focused on the large-mass distribution within the cluster, with lesser attention to smaller-mass objects that could induce significant lensing distortions. This study endeavors to incorporate the effects of these smaller-mass objects, represented by dwarf galaxies and galaxy clusters, using simulated data. We utilize a Bayesian approach to analyze the lensing distortions, accounting for the uncertainty associated with the smaller-mass objects through a predictive distribution. Subsequently, we apply a machine learning algorithm to isolate the impact of these smaller-mass objects. Initial results suggest that they produce measurable lensing effects, with strengths comparable to larger clusters. With sufficient data, we anticipate being able to pinpoint the location of dwarf galaxies, while also improving our understanding of the mass distribution within galaxy clusters.

This study explores a scenario where content is delivered via a network of internet service providers (ISPs), with each ISP located at a different point in a tree structure, and a subset of these ISPs collaborate with each other to share content investment costs. A theory is developed to analyze the equilibrium in this setting, and it's discovered that cooperative ISP relationships reduce the need for each individual ISP to invest heavily, but may ultimately lead to lower content provider profits due to reduced investment. However, if the content provider has significant market power and can impose a price on the ISPs, this cooperative effect is diminished, resulting in lower investment from the content provider and reduced profits, but only by a smaller amount, leading to increased overall welfare.

Building on the framework of categories where maps have properties of weak naturality, we establish a structure of category for these maps. This work draws inspiration from Gilbert's work on weak naturality in categories of functors, and the relationship between weak naturality and homotopy, to then define weak equivalences based on this concept. This leads to the identification of weak equivalences as a reflective property in subcategories, and ultimately, weak categories as categories with a subcategory of weak equivalences that is reflective in the original category. This work also involves characterizing strong categories as categories with a subcategory of weak equivalences that is both reflective and co-reflective.

This research investigates the potential explanations for the observed acceleration in the universe's expansion by examining a broad class of cosmological models which can be expressed through a generalized cosmological equation with specific characteristics. By analyzing the characteristics of these models, it is determined that they all feature a diverse range of cosmological solutions, with some exhibiting exponential and polynomial behaviors. To compare the models' performance, a statistical analysis is conducted, evaluating their capability to reproduce various observational data sets, including the Cosmic Microwave Background power spectrum, Baryon Acoustic Oscillation measurements, and Hubble expansion data. The results indicate that the polynomial $\beta$-attractor models provide a better fit to the data compared to their exponential counterparts. Furthermore, it is shown that these polynomial models are consistent with a diverse range of cosmological parameters, including scenarios with a finite universe and models featuring multiple phases of acceleration.

This research focuses on filling measured bending laminations as a tool to analyze quasi-Fuchsian manifolds within a specific region near the Fuchsian locus in the Teichm\"uller space. A unique quasi-Fuchsian manifold can be obtained by combining a Fuchsian manifold, a horizon curve, and a horizontal surface, where the latter two components vary continuously. However, many measured bending laminations correspond to equivalent horizons, which complicates their use in identifying quasi-Fuchsian manifolds uniquely. Despite this issue, we prove that certain conditions allow us to obtain a Fuchsian manifold and a continuous path of quasi-Fuchsian manifolds by combining a Fuchsian manifold, a filling measured bending lamination, and a nearby variant of that lamination.

This study investigates the connection between asset returns and sector-specific distributions, examining how the behavior of sector returns affects overall market returns and risk measures. A detailed analysis is presented, comparing the distribution of sector returns to that of the market, as well as how the characteristics of sector returns (mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis) correlate with corresponding market risk measures. Data from the CRSP sector index, updated quarterly from 1996 to 2016, is utilized to test hypotheses. Results support the hypothesis that sector return distributions mirror the characteristics of asset returns, providing evidence that sector returns are interconnected with asset returns. Additionally, this research explores the connection between sector risk measures to assess their interdependence.

Phonocardiography, the study of heart sounds, offers valuable insights into cardiac functions and disorders. However, recording and analyzing direct heart sounds is impractical, making indirect audio recordings from a distance the primary method used. Since these recordings are prone to noise interference from the environment, signal processing and feature extraction techniques are essential to extract reliable information. This work proposes a multi-stage deep learning approach that incorporates a sequence-to-one autoencoder for noise mitigation and a attention-based model to highlight key time segments containing vital information. Evaluations using publicly available phonocardiography datasets, specifically the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia and Cardiogram datasets, demonstrate improved detection accuracy when using the proposed method against existing alternatives. Furthermore, we present a graphical implementation of the model using a Temporal Convolutional Network that achieves accurate PPG and heart sound analysis.

A theoretical analysis enhancing the predictions for electric dipole transition probabilities in isospin asymmetric nuclei via the RPA is presented. The findings suggest that the Main, Core, and Tail components play distinct roles in evaluating these transition probabilities. It's observed that while the Main and Core contributions primarily make up the total transition amplitude, the Tail component's influence is minimal. Furthermore, the study reveals that the Tail contribution is mainly significant at energies corresponding to the Giant Isospin Magnetic Dipole Resonance.

Let $G$ be a finite group that acts effectively on the 2-torus, $T^2$, by homeomorphisms, and consider a map $G$ acts on the loop space of $T^2$, and let ${\rm Map}_*(T^2, {\rm Lie} G)$ represent the space of oriented degree-$*$ maps from $T^2$ to the Lie group $G$ equipped with an orienting vector. Applying the Satake homomorphism yields an equivariant cohomology relation that involves the cohomology of $T^2$ and ${\rm Map}_*(T^2, {\rm Lie} G)$. Furthermore, we find that this connection can be described by a chain complex that effectively simulates the action of $G$ on $T^2$ and provides insights into the twists in the action. Ultimately, we calculate the equivariant cohomology of the torus for all possible effective actions of a finite group, and we determine the twists in the action for a specific $G$ that acts on the torus in a particular way.

This study investigates the outcomes of strategic interventions designed to foster
a more unified, collaborative, and inclusive academic environment within a research
department at a leading technical institution. Intended to boost teamwork and promote
equity, these initiatives encompassed multiple aspects including communication,
work-life balance, and diversity. To gauge their effectiveness, a comprehensive evaluation
was performed, encompassing both perception surveys and in-depth interviews with the
entire department staff. The analysis reveals that while the staff acknowledge and give
credit to the efforts made to improve the work atmosphere, the tangible benefits in terms
of collaboration and inclusion are still limited. Crucially, it is evident that sustained
efforts are necessary to address the underlying, deeply rooted issues that currently hinder
the staff's full engagement and a more unified, inclusive culture can only be achieved by
addressing these fundamental problems.

This paper investigates the fractional series operator's mapping properties between $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$. It is demonstrated that the operator $T_{\lambda}$ is not necessarily bounded from $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ into $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ for $1<p<q<\infty$, unless certain conditions such as $\lambda = \gamma/2$ and $p \geq q$ are met, given that $\gamma$ is a positive real number. Under the condition $\lambda = \gamma/2$, the norm of the operator $T_{\lambda}: H^{p}(\mathbb{Z}) \to H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$ is maximized and can be expressed as $q/(p-1)$ under the norm defined by the maximal function.

This study investigates how the actions of bidders in online auctions can be influenced by various factors, with a specific focus on how the rules of the auction are structured. It distinguishes between a controlled environment where auction participants can be modeled as playing a comprehensive, strategic game and an uncontrolled setting, such as the observed data generated through the application of best response strategies by individual bidders. Building on prior research, this paper formalizes the concept of a revenue maximization principle for participants in auctions that are not bound by a set of predetermined rules. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the application of this principle results in observed data that is consistent with theories that account for the cost of participation and the consequences of breaking auction rules. In particular, this research reveals that the reason sellers in online auctions do not always maximize their revenue is due to a complex interplay of factors, including the cost of participation, the probability of being caught breaking auction rules, and the willingness of competitors to invest in avoiding rule violations. It is further shown that the difference between a revenue-maximizing bid that is not bound by rules and the actual bid submitted by participants is directly proportional to the perceived probability of being caught breaking those rules. In addition, this research provides estimates of the level of enforcement of rules in the context of freeparking.com auctions, with results indicating that the probability of being caught violating rules on this platform is approximately 0.96.

We investigate how geometric anisotropy in the early universe evolves from a state of extreme anisotropy to isotropy over time. This research builds upon a previous study (arXiv:2202.04445) that introduced a novel mechanism underlying this phenomenon, involving a complex scalar field interacting with gravity in a specific manner. In this work, we refine our theoretical framework and explore its implications using the Bianchi type-I model. Our findings demonstrate that as the universe's anisotropy decreases, causing it to resemble a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker model, a finite amount of energy is released, corresponding to the anisotropy's rate of decay. This energy is distributed uniformly throughout the universe, leading to a scale-invariant primordial density fluctuation spectrum, thus providing a theoretical basis for the cosmic microwave background's features. In contrast to inflationary models, our findings indicate that this phenomenon occurs naturally without the necessity of fine-tuning.

This paper delves into Gr\"obner fan technology in relation to Hessenberg varieties, specifically the Gr\"obner fan associated with the local Gr\"obner fans that parameterize the Gr\"obner varieties representing extremal Gr\"obner vectors from certain families related to Hessenberg varieties. Local Gr\"obner fans are three-dimensional and are connected to Fock-Gross-Kogan variates, which describe limiting points of reduced words in the Weyl group, tied to the structure of partially ordered partitions. The study constructs Gr\"obner fan coordinates by resolving an integral polyhedral structure, which leads to the development of an algorithm for identifying the closure of any point within a local Gr\"obner fan. This combinatorial approach is used to verify specific properties, such as the presence of smooth points, the resolution of singularities, and the description of tangent spaces. Additionally, the work presents explicit examples illustrating the complexity of Gr\"obner fan geometry.

This paper introduces a novel approach to generating full brushstrokes in paintings
using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), building on a prior technique that created
individual paint marks. By leveraging conditional GANs, we developed a model capable
of learning stroke synthesis from existing paintings and applying it to generate new
works of art. To achieve this, we established a database of simple brushstrokes called
"BrushData" and used it to create more complex composition models. We also conducted
experiments on existing painting datasets, presenting generated brushstrokes and
compositions alongside existing method outcomes in the accompanying website.

We examine current data on flavor anomalies within particle physics to assess potential signs of new physics at low energy levels. Focusing on the systematic uncertainties inherent in these phenomena, particularly in the universality of lepton-flavor interactions as exemplified by the results from LHCb and Belle experiments, we emphasize the significance of direct reconstruction in statistical analyses to account for experimental biases when dealing with events influenced by charm quarks. We demonstrate that even a slight improvement in the experimental uncertainty on the curation of events can substantially affect the 95% confidence level (C.L.) limits on potential new physics parameters, often translating to a feasible resolution by the time experimental data is expected to be upgraded to 2024, as forecasted by predictions.

Conversational Question Answering (CQA) is a vital language understanding capability.
Past methods have focused on using semantic parsing to convert questions into logical forms,
but struggled with generating correct phrases to address questions.
Our research reveals that this challenge lies in retaining both question and context information.
To overcome this, we've developed a new dataset called QASPER which expands upon the existing SQuAD dataset by including more questions and richer contextual information.
Additionally, we've created a new model called QAFormer which uses transformer architecture to integrate question and context information.
By leveraging multi-head attention, our model enables cross-dependent information to be captured.
Both human evaluations and performance metrics show QAFormer to outperform previous approaches on SQuAD and achieve near-human performance on QASPER!

The core collapse of a massive star leads to its explosive transformation into a supernova, a phenomenon whose processes have not been fully elucidated yet. Using advanced simulations, researchers have studied the mechanics of a fast-moving shock wave inside the star. They found that inside the star, this shock wave causes rapid movement of gas and formulates a model to explain its behavior. The model indicates that the impact of the star's explosion or collapse is a significant determining factor in whether a fast-moving instability occurs in the shock wave. The study has shown that inside the star, a steady and smooth shock wave exists, but outside it, irregular patterns can occur depending on various factors, such as the star's angular momentum and its position relative to the core. These irregular patterns cause rapid movement of gas and lead to the formation of a specific structure in the star. The study has also found that outside the star, a fast-moving instability occurs only if the explosion occurs with a certain level of intensity, a phenomenon not seen in simulations of collapsing stars with lower levels of angular momentum and not observed in real-life supernovae either. The study has shown that outside the star, a fast-moving instability occurs only if certain specific conditions are met, a phenomenon not seen in other types of stellar collapses and not observed in real-life supernovae either. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, a neurodevelopmental disorder, lacks distinctive biomarkers in children. Current research relies heavily on subjective evaluations by experts, increasing the need for automated and efficient diagnosis methods. In this study, a novel deep neural network based on ResNet-50 and attention mechanism was developed to identify ADHD from an EEG dataset. The model's performance improved significantly after being re-engineered with a novel attention mechanism based on region of interest data. When trained on reduced datasets consisting of important regions of interest, the model achieved impressive test accuracy of 70.46% on the ITSW dataset and 70.83% on the CHB2013 dataset, showcasing the efficacy of targeted training strategies. Additionally, the model's novel attention mechanism was analyzed and compared to other existing approaches using gradient, saliency, and attention-based methods.

We demonstrate the uniqueness of the interior fixed point for the Frostmann integral operator with respect to the L^p metric (1 < p < infinity). This operator is commonly used in financial modeling to compute the value of a cash balance investment strategy under the assumption that a company's cash balance strategy follows a Poisson process with certain parameters. The operator's fixed point represents a stationary cash balance strategy that is optimal under the Black and Scholes framework. The uniqueness of the interior fixed point is crucial for developing this strategy.

Acronyms are widespread in written language, often consisting of smaller words and
relating to specific domains, with their expansions sometimes unclear or difficult
to identify. This study focuses on developing a system capable of identifying and
disambiguating acronyms across various domains and writing styles. By analyzing large
text datasets, the system learns to recognize when an acronym might be present, and
then uses contextual clues within a limited surrounding text area to determine its
expansion. This study showcases the system's performance on two major datasets, one
focusing on medical text and another on technical acronyms.

This study explores the possibility of heat rectification in quantum Hall systems, employing a nano-electrical device located at a Torah point where the Hall conductivity is quantized yet non-spontaneous counter-currents occur. We propose a protocol to induce a directional heat flow, facilitated by a low-ohmic connection, which allows a thermal resistor to modulate the Hall conductor's heat transmission. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the system can effectively rectify heat by up to 90% efficiency. Additionally, we investigate how to enhance the rectification effect by adjusting a gate that controls the Hall conductor's filling factor.

The implementation of DNA data storage, a promising new technology, has been hindered by the lack of effective methods for managing storage compartments where DNA data is encoded. Research has mainly focused on the issue of errors that occur during DNA reading, but the problem of storage space efficiency due to the varying sizes of primer pairs has been overlooked until now. In this study, we develop mathematical models to describe primer pair design and these sub-compartments, and use computational tools like the NSPA to optimize primer pairs based on size, alignment, and coverage considerations. Experimental results show that our approach leads to a significant reduction - up to 37% less space is needed - which means more data can be stored in the same amount of space. In real-world terms, this means an increase of 7 to 10 times in data storage capacity using our improved primer design technique.

Topological states in two-dimensional systems exhibit unique characteristics in their boundary areas. The recently proposed theory of topological semimetals describes a particular situation where the entire semimetallic state is confined to a single line in the momentum space, encompassing an infinite plane. This nodal line topological state may exhibit topological characteristics in a surrounding surface area rather than throughout the entire bulk. We explore the properties of this nodal line topological state, its theoretical framework, and potential examples, as well as the distinct behaviors exhibited when it is subjected to an external influence of charge, magnetic field, and light.

Researchers examined whether an oscillating system could maintain a constant wave speed by investigating whether the peak velocity of a wave triggered by an oscillator depends on the peak velocity of the inducing oscillator. They conducted this investigation by analyzing simulations featuring a pair of interacting oscillators aligned along a straight line and located at a distance of approximately five times the distance a wave travels in a given time period. The distance between the two oscillators was incrementally increased while recording the velocity of the wave triggered by each oscillator. The study found that this velocity was consistent with a power law and showed that the interaction between the two oscillators results in a wave speed that is comparable to the speed of waves in less interactive systems. However, the study also discovered that the wave speed is influenced by the distance between the two oscillators and found that this distance has a significant impact at close range. Further analysis revealed that the wave speed is influenced by the distance between the two oscillators and found that this distance has a significant impact at close range. The study found that this distance has a significant impact at close range.

To measure the amount of uncertainty in a data source that follows a specific probability distribution, researchers use an estimate called min-entropy. This estimate is calculated by first finding upper and lower bounds of the entropic value by analyzing samples from the data source, then using these bounds to calculate the amount of uncertainty, provided that the average uncertainty is greater than zero. If this condition isn't met, researchers use a modified approach that involves adjusting the inequality. This new approach is the first to provide an efficient way of calculating minimum entropy in the context of continuous distributions, doing so with an amount of data that grows linearly. This theoretical advancement is demonstrated with practical applications, including one where a commonly used metric in data analysis is shown to be an inadequate measure of uncertainty when compared to the new minimum entropy approach.

Creating a comprehensive imaging biobank with the potential for significant advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) healthcare requires careful planning. This involves establishing a secure, decentralized system for storing and accessing protected health information, as well as implementing robust access controls and data protection measures. Furthermore, as AI technologies evolve, imaging biobanks must be designed to integrate seamlessly with emerging systems easily. To address these challenges, this paper examines the technical implications of creating a next-generation imaging biobank, beginning with the design of its underlying software infrastructure. We will then examine security, access, and data management concerns, presenting novel solutions to complex problems in the process. As AI applications continue to shift from centralized to distributed systems, such as cloud and edge computing environments, our discussion will explore how imaging biobanks can effectively utilize these platforms effectively. To facilitate replication of our results, all software development tasks have been completed using open-source methods and are available for review at github.com/kairosai/imbiolibank.

Current deep learning models for diagnosing and interpreting medical images rely heavily on data augmentation methods like horizontal flipping. However, the effectiveness of these methods is often linked to the presence of clinical features, such as patient demographics and medical history, which are only available in certain cases. In this study, we examine the efficacy of data augmentation methods in the context of deep learning-based medical image diagnosis and patient characterization. By integrating multiple clinical features, we found that data augmentation could significantly improve the accuracy of patient characterization, while only slightly enhancing diagnosis. Moreover, the best results were achieved by combining multiple data augmentation techniques, such as flipping and resizing, rather than relying on automatic region-based methods like DenseLayer. This highlights the importance of carefully selecting data augmentation strategies based on the problem at hand. This research was conducted using the publicly available MS-COCO-12k dataset.

Polymatroidal ideals, defined as ideals that remain unchanged under a specific transformation in their associated multigraded free resolutions, have significant implications in the polymatroid theory and algebraic geometry. This transformation, known as the matroid mutation operation, is not only linear but also satisfies a certain duality property. When applied to a polymatroidal ideal, this operation yields another polymatroidal ideal, whose primary feature is that their sum remains a polymatroidal ideal. This result extends a previous finding for specific types of polymatroidal ideals and can be used to establish a connection between the polymatroidal and toric complete intersection cones.

We develop a quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm by integrating classical K-means with quantum techniques utilizing unitary operators and the qunet approach from prior research. This integration yields a quantum proximity protocol that we embed within a larger clustering process. The proposed protocol achieves efficient logarithmic scaling in its qubit and query complexities, surpassing classical asymptotics.
